title: Development of an epigenetic marker panel for the classification of alcohol consumption habits
summary: Alcohol consumption is a common cause of illness worldwide and also plays an important role in criminal offenses. When people are asked about their alcohol consumption, their answers are often unreliable—whether due to forgetfulness, denial, or fear of legal consequences. The latter could be the case, for example, when it comes to questions of criminal responsibility or driving ability. Although considerable research efforts have been made in recent decades to objectify a person's alcohol consumption, established alcohol consumption markers have relevant limitations. For example, they often only provide information about consumption in the preceding days, require special body samples such as hair, or can be easily distorted by other factors such as liver disease. Reliable long-term markers, i.e., measurements in the body that provide meaningful information about alcohol consumption behavior over many weeks or months, are therefore only available to a very limited extent. There is therefore still a great need for innovative alcohol consumption markers. In recent years, scientists have been investigating whether alcohol consumption can also be detected via so-called epigenetic changes. In other words: Does the environmental factor of alcohol consumption alter the reading of a specific blueprint of the body's cells without changing the genetic information itself? Such changes could, for example, involve the altered attachment of small chemical groups to the genetic material (DNA methylation)  or a change in the amount of tiny messenger molecules (e. g. miRNA) in the body. Similar effects have already been observed with other environmental influences such as smoking. Initial data from very large-scale studies also suggest corresponding changes in the blood for alcohol consumption. However, there is a lack of studies that examine whether these changes can actually be used as a “tool” to classify a person's alcohol consumption behavior. This research project aims to investigate this question. Of particular interest to the research would be not only changes in the blood, but also in the oral mucosa. Samples could be taken particularly easily from the oral mucosa. Blood and oral mucosa samples from volunteer test subjects will therefore be examined to determine whether alcohol consumption actually causes corresponding changes and whether these changes are reversible. Test subjects who either drink alcohol regularly or do not drink alcohol at all will be recruited for this purpose. Their consumption will also be monitored using questionnaires, special blood tests, and, if necessary, a drinking diary. After a period of abstinence, the researchers will examine whether and how the measurements have changed compared to before abstinence and whether there are differences between blood and cheek mucosa tissue. The data generated in this way will be used to develop a mathematical model. The long-term goal is to develop a marker panel—i.e., a combination of several changes that reliably correlate with alcohol consumption habits—that can be used to reliably objectify the alcohol consumption behavior of individuals outside the study. Among other things, this would be helpful for health care and research applications, but could also be useful for answering numerous specific questions in legal and traffic medicine.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Written informed consent has been obtained. “Continuous” alcohol consumption behavior (according to AUDIT-C with low, moderate or high risk for classification into cohorts with no, moderate and high consumption).
Exclusion criteria:
Age <18 years, high alcohol consumption without current qualified withdrawal, current polytoxicomania, known alcohol metabolism disorder, severe acute cardiovascular, respiratory, renal or coagulation disorder requiring treatment, poor blood vessel conditions in the arms, inability to give consent.
